# Leaderboard (generated by `python -m bmtbench.report`, protocol v1 + amendments A1-A5)

Data: Binance Vision spot 1h archives (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, attribution: Binance Vision; not affiliated with or endorsed by
Binance). These tables are derived from that data and carry the same licence. Research evaluation only.

Rows: 393,407 hourly and 80,307 daily forecast origins, 62 assets with rows (47 trained-on, 15 never trained on; two of the 17 held-out symbols were delisted before 2023), four unseen calendar
folds 2023-01 .. 2026-10. Every model is scored on the same rows. `sPL` = asset-equal scaled pinball over 21 quantiles (lower is
better). Intervals are 95 % block-bootstrap (weekly / 4-weekly calendar blocks, 1,000 resamples); skills against a reference
are paired. `bmt-*` = this project's candidates (`-sym` = 2-pass flip-averaged, `-x` = BTC covariate + calendar inputs, sizes
t / s / m = 0.11M / 0.81M / 4.8M parameters), one model per fold trained only on data ending 104 days before the fold.

## Reading it

- Does a candidate beat Timestral on unseen folds? Yes, by a small margin that the paired intervals separate from zero at every
  hourly horizon and at daily h = 1, on trained-on and never-trained-on assets alike. Against the reference Timestral pipeline
  (512 context) the 0.11M `bmt-t` gains 0.56 % (h 1), 0.42 % (h 6), 0.88 % (h 24) hourly and 0.39 % daily h 1; it is also
  separated in the latest fold (F4) at each of those and on BTC alone at the hourly horizons (not on BTC daily). Daily h 5 is
  not separated for the univariate models (`bmt-s-x-sym`: 0.67 % [0.30, 1.06]). Some single-pass variants lose the F4
  separation at h 1 (`bmt-s`: 0.30 % [-0.01, 0.66]).
- Against the production contract (`timestral-fast`, the 256-context one-step kernel) the gain is 1.4-1.5 % at every hourly horizon.
- Against Timestral's best configuration found here (2,048-bar context) the gain shrinks to 0.4-0.5 % at h 1 and to 0.1-0.2 % at
  h 6 / h 24, where `bmt-t` is no longer separated from it. Longer context is the obvious next input for the candidates too.
- Scale of the whole contest: the best model is 4.1 % better than a Gaussian random walk at hourly h 1. GARCH(1,1)-t is within
  0.3 % of the reference Timestral pipeline at the hourly horizons (0.5-0.8 % behind on daily). Chronos-2 fed log prices is worse than the random walk at h 1 and h 24; fed returns it matches
  `timestral-fast` at h 1.
- Point forecasts: the candidates' medians have a small edge that the foundation models do not show. Hourly, `bmt-t` has
  relMAE vs the zero forecast 0.9972 [0.9958, 0.9986] at h 1 (0.998 at h 6 and h 24), directional accuracy 52.8 % [52.2, 53.4]
  at h 1 (51.6 % / 51.2 % at h 6 / h 24) and a mean cross-sectional rank IC of 0.065 / 0.051 / 0.041, against 1.0018, 51.1 %
  and 0.025 for `timestral-official` (`timestral-fast`: 1.008, 49.6 %, -0.011). It holds on the never-trained-on assets. On
  daily bars relMAE and directional accuracy are not separated from 1 and 50 % (IC about 0.065). The IC has no interval here,
  and an hourly close-to-close effect of this size may be bid-ask bounce: it says nothing about PnL after costs.
- Size and data curves are flat (below): 0.11M parameters and 5 % of the training symbols already give the same score.
- Seen vs unseen assets: no gap. Candidates are as good on the 17 symbols they never trained on.
- An average of `bmt-s-sym` and `timestral-official` quantiles is not better than `bmt-s-sym` alone.
- Caveats: Timestral's and Chronos-2's pretraining data and cut-offs are not disclosed, so older folds may be in-sample for
  them (this favours them); the candidates' recipe was chosen with F1 / F3 test numbers visible (amendment A4); the placebo
  failed its pre-registered form at one horizon (below); one data source, one exchange, spot only.

## Speed

One row = one 512-bar context -> 4 horizons x 21 quantiles for `bmt` (24 steps x 21 for the reference pipelines, one horizon for
the `tsfm16` kernel). RTX 5090 shared with production servers (their load at the start of each run is in the last column; numbers
move +-30 % with it and are lower bounds), CPU = Xeon E5-2697 v4 (AVX2, no AVX-512) on a host at load average about 80 of 72
threads. Host-device transfer and the pipe round trip are included. Timed calls: 30-200, fewer for calls over a second.
Mojo-vs-PyTorch parity of the candidates: max error 1.8e-6 (CPU) / 6.5e-6 (GPU) scale units on the self-test vector, tolerance 2e-4.

{{SPEED}}

At batch 4096 the Mojo GPU path forwards `bmt-s` 17x faster than `timestral-fast` and 48x faster than `timestral-max`
(`bmt-t`: 32x / 87x); `bmt-t` on 12 CPU threads is twice as fast as `timestral-fast` on the GPU. Batch-1 latency is launch
overhead for every GPU path (2-4 ms for `bmt`, 4-9 ms for `tsfm16`, 60-90 ms for the PyTorch pipelines); on CPU `bmt-t` answers
a single row in 0.28 ms.

## Learning curve (fold F4)

{{LC}}

Size m at 5 % / 25 % was not run (the first attempt hit this task's VRAM cap). Validation score = mean over horizons of
sPL / sqrt(h) on the 90 days before the fold.

## Leakage checks

- Timestamp audit, causality test, unseen-symbol exclusion, sampler purge: `tests/test_leakage.py`, passing; the last training
  target bar of every fold is stored in the prediction metadata (104 days before the test period).
- Shuffled-time placebo (`bmt-s` retrained and scored on time-permuted returns):

{{PLACEBO}}

  The pre-registered form fails at hourly h = 24 because the `empirical` reference is weak there (the Gaussian `naive` beats it
  by 2.75 % on the same permuted data), not because the candidate knows the future: against the better unconditional baseline
  its edge is 0.37 %. See amendment A1 in `PROTOCOL.md`. Stated plainly: as written before the results, the check did not pass.
